title: Blessings and Curses of the Covenant
lead: Deuteronomy sets before Israel "a blessing and a curse": the good that follows listening to God, and the disaster that follows turning to other gods. Like ancient treaties, it ends its laws with blessings and curses (chapters 27–28), and the prophets and Paul read Israel's history and Christ's death through them.

sections.h: Blessing and curse in the covenant
sections.b: The pairing of blessing and curse runs from God's promise to Abraham, "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever treats you with contempt I will curse" (Genesis 12:3), to the covenant lists of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. Deuteronomy sets the two before Israel as a choice (Deuteronomy 11:26–28; Deuteronomy 30:15–20), and Joshua carries out the ceremony at Mount Ebal (Joshua 8:30–35). The prophets read the exile as the curses coming true (2 Kings 17:7–23; Daniel 9:11). Jesus' blessings and woes (Luke 6:20–26) take up the same pattern, and Paul says Christ became a curse to bring Abraham's blessing to the nations (Galatians 3:10–14). Revelation 22:3 promises that there will be no more curse.
